note: Original editorial descriptions written from publicly reported facts (never copied from the Michelin Guide or reviews). Point-in-time; verify before treating chef/menu specifics as current.

addison-san-diego-ca.text: San Diego's first three-Michelin-star restaurant, Addison sits on a Carmel Valley hillside inside the Fairmont Grand Del Mar, its dining room framed by high ceilings and arched windows. Chef William Bradley builds a ten-course, season-driven menu that runs French technique through California ingredients, with playful turns — a churro filled with chicken liver, Kennebec chips with burnt-onion dip and a caviar-topped china sunflower, shellfish chawanmushi. A 10,000-bottle cellar of small producers and rare Champagnes rounds out one of the country's most polished tasting-menu experiences.

benu-san-francisco-ca.text: When Corey Lee opened Benu in 2010, it became the first San Francisco restaurant to hold three Michelin stars. In a minimalist 40-seat SoMa room, Lee gives Asian cooking a French-precise, deeply technical spin — the kitchen's famous "thousand-year-old" quail egg, a lobster-coral xiao long bao with tissue-thin skin, whole roasted quail glazed in maple and soy and carved tableside. Korean and Chinese ideas meet exacting classical technique in a menu that helped redefine modern American fine dining.

carino-chicago-il.text: Tucked beneath the Red Line tracks in Chicago's Uptown — next door to a hair salon — Cariño is chef Norman Fenton's love letter to Mexico. Fenton fell for the country on a nine-month road trip and later ran the kitchen at WILD Tulum; here he channels that immersion into a 12-to-16-course Latin-American tasting menu with a heavy Mexican accent, served to just seven seats at the chef's counter. It opens with a wink — "chips and salsa" reimagined as salsa verde jelly and tortilla crumble — and only gets bolder. A Michelin star, a Banchet Best New Restaurant award, and a James Beard nod have followed; night owls can catch the late-night taco omakase, Wednesday through Saturday at 9:30.

holbox-los-angeles-ca.text: Inside Mercado La Paloma, a former garment factory turned South LA market, Holbox is the country's only Michelin-starred Mexican marisquería. Chef Gilberto Cetina — a three-time James Beard nominee — draws on Mexico's coasts, especially the Yucatán, working sustainably sourced Southern California seafood with lime, tomato, habanero and cilantro. Ceviches of rockfish and kanpachi, wild Mexican shrimp served in a goblet, a velvety red seafood stew and the signature octopus taco have made this counter one of Los Angeles's most beloved tables.

kasama-chicago-il.text: Opened in 2020 by chef-partners Genie Kwon and Tim Flores, Kasama made history as the first Filipino restaurant in the United States to earn a Michelin star — and now holds two. In Chicago's West Town it leads a deliberate double life: a counter-service bakery by day, turning out Filipino pastries and breakfast plates, and a reservation-only tasting menu by night. Kwon's acclaimed pastry work and Flores's savory cooking drive the $325 dinner, with wine or non-alcoholic pairings, which has also earned a James Beard Award and a place among North America's 50 Best. Equal parts neighborhood bakery and long-planned destination, it rewards a casual morning pastry as much as a milestone dinner.

le-bernardin-new-york-ny.text: Born in Paris in 1972 and transplanted to New York in 1986, Le Bernardin has spent decades as the city's definitive seafood restaurant, holding three Michelin stars under chef Eric Ripert. The kitchen honors the fish above all: an à la carte menu organized into "Almost Raw" and "Lightly Cooked" refuses to force guests into a marathon tasting. Signatures like the pounded-thin yellowfin tuna laid over toasted baguette and foie gras distill Ripert's philosophy — French technique, global inspiration, and the purity of the ingredient.

lilo-carlsbad-ca.text: Lilo earned a Michelin star within ten weeks of opening in 2025 — a near-unheard-of ascent for a 22-seat Carlsbad newcomer from chef Eric Bost and restaurateur John Resnick. Bost draws on the Southern California coast, with detours through France, Japan and other kindred coastal cuisines, across a $265 menu of many small, meticulous courses rather than large plates. Dishes like spot prawns in a sauce of sea buckthorn, lime leaf, serrano and gooseberry show the kitchen's precise, produce-driven hand.

mutra-north-miami-fl.text: In a North Miami strip mall, Mutra made history as the first kosher restaurant anywhere to earn a Michelin star. Named for chef Raz Shabtai's late grandmother, it channels the multicultural food traditions of Jerusalem — with threads from North Africa, Eastern Europe and the Levant — into a frequently changing, farm-to-table menu served at an intimate chef's counter. Inspectors singled out its "One Perfect Falafel," a beet dish set in ajo blanco with beetroot sorbet, the signature lamb kebab with smoked eggplant cream, and a rosewater muhallebi to finish.

the-french-laundry-yountville-ca.text: Thomas Keller's French Laundry has anchored American fine dining from its Yountville stone cottage since 1994, holding three Michelin stars for progressive American cooking rooted in classic French technique. Its opening sequence is close to sacred: "Oysters and Pearls," a sabayon of tapioca pearls with poached oysters and caviar, is a course that never changes. Keller's farm-to-table, regional-sourcing ethos set a template that much of the country's high-end cooking still follows.

yingtao-new-york-ny.text: Named for owner Bolun Yao's grandmother, YingTao is the only Michelin-starred Chinese tasting-menu restaurant in New York — a star earned within a year of its 2023 opening by the husband-and-wife team of Bolun and Linette Yao. In a Hell's Kitchen room of black marble, brass and scarlet cherry accents, chef Emily Yuen — a James Beard semifinalist whose résumé spans Michelin kitchens in London, Australia and Singapore — reframes Chinese cooking through contemporary fine dining. The seasonal seven-course, $150 menu trades takeout clichés for philosophy, technique and storytelling.

smyth-chicago-il.text: The passion project of husband-and-wife chefs John Shields and Karen Urie Shields — alumni of Alinea, Tru and Charlie Trotter's — Smyth turns three decades of experience toward North American farmers, fishermen and makers at the peak of their season. In the West Loop, the daily-changing $420 tasting menu treats pristine product as the whole point: lobster custard with raspberry butter and a poached claw, a quail egg cured in black walnut miso, caramelized butternut squash with sikil pak. Named No. 1 on North America's 50 Best in 2026, it pairs with the couple's more casual downstairs sibling, The Loyalist.

singlethread-healdsburg-ca.text: SingleThread is a farm, restaurant and five-room inn woven into one experience by chef Kyle Connaughton and farmer Katina Connaughton in downtown Healdsburg. A 24-acre Dry Creek Valley farm supplies the vegetables, fruit, herbs and honey behind a ten-course, kaiseki-influenced menu shaped by the couple's years in Japan — an opening "botanical landscape" of first bites, precise knife work, and the signature donabe clay pot that transforms seafood and vegetables. Inn guests can trade the tasting menu for a family-style donabe hot-pot dinner served in their room.

providence-los-angeles-ca.text: Open since 2005, Michael Cimarusti's Providence is Los Angeles's temple to sustainable seafood — one of the first two restaurants in Greater LA to reach three Michelin stars, and holder of a Green Star for its sourcing. Cimarusti treats pristine, often wild-caught fish with classical French finesse across contemporary tasting menus; the signature is Santa Barbara uni set over a decadent egg yolk, alongside a celebrated caviar service. It is among the most decorated kitchens in the country, and a standard-bearer for the chef-as-conservationist.

eleven-madison-park-new-york-ny.text: Daniel Humm's Eleven Madison Park overlooks its namesake Manhattan park from a grand Art Deco room, and in 2021 it made history as the first entirely plant-based restaurant to hold three Michelin stars. Humm rebuilt the menu around vegetables and invention — a crisp vegan roll with fermented sunflower "butter," a tonburi quenelle mimicking caviar with horseradish cream — keeping its stars along the way. The kitchen has more recently begun reintroducing meat and duck options alongside the plant-based tasting. It remains one of New York's defining fine-dining destinations.

jungsik-new-york-new-york-ny.text: Opened in Tribeca in 2011 by Seoul-born chef Jungsik Yim, Jungsik pioneered a "New Korean" fine dining and, in 2024, became the first Korean restaurant in the United States to earn three Michelin stars — New York's first new three-star in twelve years. A single elegant tasting menu (from about $295, under executive chef Daeik Kim) reinterprets Korean flavors with precision: raw striped jack with white kimchi and chilled fish-bone broth, crisp octopus with gochujang aioli, dry-aged Arctic char in kimchi and red curry. It laid the groundwork for Korean fine dining's rise in America.

per-se-new-york-ny.text: Thomas Keller's New York counterpart to The French Laundry, Per Se has held three Michelin stars since the city's first guide in 2006, perched above Columbus Circle with sweeping Central Park views. Built on the French Laundry's foundation — Keller closed the Yountville flagship for five months to train the team — it serves a daily nine-course tasting, plus a nine-course vegetable menu, of classic French technique and impeccable product. The meal opens, as ever, with "Oysters and Pearls," a sabayon of tapioca pearls with poached oysters and caviar.

sushi-sho-new-york-ny.text: Sushi Sho brought master Keiji Nakazawa's revered Edomae omakase to Midtown Manhattan in 2024, and within a year it became the only sushi restaurant in the U.S. to hold three Michelin stars. Nakazawa — who ran the original Sushi Sho in Tokyo's Yotsuya for more than thirty years — champions the 19th-century Edomae style, curing, simmering and marinating fish rather than serving it merely raw to coax out deeper flavor. The result is a traditional, deeply expressive counter experience rooted in the very origins of sushi.

atelier-crenn-san-francisco-ca.text: At Atelier Crenn, Dominique Crenn became the first female chef in the U.S. to earn three Michelin stars, in 2018. Her deeply personal "poetic culinaria" — the menu has famously read as a poem — traces a journey from her seaside childhood in Brittany to the Pacific, built on pescatarian and plant courses with much of the produce grown at her own Bleu Belle Farm in Sonoma. Seafood, delicate sauces and farm vegetables meet in cooking that is at once indulgent and nourishing, and unmistakably autobiographical.

californios-san-francisco-ca.text: Val Cantú's Californios began as a pop-up and, in 2026, became the first Mexican restaurant in the world to earn three Michelin stars. From its SoMa home the kitchen sends out a roughly 16-course, ~$375 tasting rooted in Cantú's family traditions and his grandmother's cooking, using sustainable ingredients from small California farms — uni-caviar sopes, a matsukasa-yaki fish taco, rack of lamb with mole amarillo and morels. Michelin praised its precision and clarity "without losing the Mexican identity," a landmark for Mexican fine dining.

quince-san-francisco-ca.text: Opened in 2003 by Michael and Lindsay Tusk and in Jackson Square since 2009, Quince is a San Francisco institution that climbed to three Michelin stars in 2017. Tusk's Californian cooking runs on Italian and French technique and Northern California produce, with handmade pasta a perennial highlight — agnolotti of white asparagus, first-of-season peas in a guanciale-and-clam broth. Refined and quietly luxurious, it anchors the Tusks' family of restaurants alongside Cotogna and Verjus.

enclos-sonoma-ca.text: Enclos opened in Sonoma in December 2024 and rose meteorically — two Michelin stars in 2025, three in 2026. Chef Brian Limoges reworks memories of his New Hampshire upbringing into refined eight-to-ten-course tasting menus — a lobster-roll croustade, clam-chowder chawanmushi — built on produce from Stone Edge Farm's carbon-negative estate gardens. The kitchen's regenerative ethos runs deep, even repurposing fallen trees into chopsticks and serving trays, blending California bounty with New England nostalgia.

somni-west-hollywood-ca.text: Somni — Catalan for "dream" — is Aitor Zabala's intimate counter in West Hollywood, and in 2025 it became the first restaurant in Greater Los Angeles to earn three Michelin stars. Zabala, who apprenticed under José Andrés in Barcelona, sends a long, endlessly creative procession of small bites across a contemporary Spanish menu shaped by California: mussel escabeche, gazpacho, an iconic shiso-tartare tempura. Reopened in 2024 after its original Beverly Hills location closed during the pandemic, its handful of seats are among the hardest to get in LA.

alinea-chicago-il.text: Grant Achatz and Nick Kokonas's Alinea is American avant-garde dining at its most theatrical — a maximalist, modernist experience of scented vapors, hidden ingredients and tableside surprise. Long a three-star fixture (2011–2024) before settling at two, it remains one of Chicago's most immersive tables: "pearls" of spiced orange, an edible green-apple-and-helium balloon, and a finale painted directly onto the tabletop as an edible canvas. Whimsy and precision in equal measure, it helped define the genre.

ever-chicago-il.text: Curtis Duffy and partner Michael Muser's Ever occupies a sleek, futuristic Fulton Market room — familiar to viewers of The Bear — where Duffy's ingredient-led cooking turns technical precision into quiet drama. Choose the 12- or 15-course menu, one seafood-and-protein and one vegetable-forward: Ora King salmon with fennel, a tom kha gai hidden under crisped rice and fried chicken skin with fragrant coconut broth poured tableside, wagyu with braised pistachio. It is refined, modern American cooking with a designer's eye for presentation.

oriole-chicago-il.text: Reached through a converted freight elevator in a covert West Loop alley, Oriole is Noah Sandoval's tasting-menu-only hideaway — a former warehouse with a striking ceiling collage over its spotless open kitchen. The long menu blends French and Japanese sensibilities and opens with a luxe salvo of finger food: scallop, jamón ibérico, sea urchin, prawn and caviar. Foie gras with California fig and a restrained black-truffle capellini show a kitchen equally capable of opulence and self-control.

aska-brooklyn-ny.text: Aska — Swedish for "ashes" — is Stockholm-born Fredrik Berselius's New Nordic table in Brooklyn, grown from his earlier pop-up Frej into a two-star destination. Around an open kitchen, a small team sends out a 12-to-16-course menu rooted in foraging, preservation, smoke and seasonality: langoustine with violets, a potato pancake with roe emulsion, and the signature mushroom-fudge-filled æbleskiver with woodruff syrup. Wild herbs, berries and pristine seafood give the meal a Nordic soul without dogma.

atomix-new-york-ny.text: Junghyun "JP" Park and his wife and partner Ellia built Atomix into one of the world's most acclaimed Korean restaurants — No. 6 on the World's 50 Best in 2024, the highest-ranked U.S. restaurant that year. Just twelve seats ring a U-shaped counter in NoMad, where a ten-course "New Korean" menu arrives with collectible ceramics and illustrated cards: gim seaweed rice cake with trout roe and perilla, galbi with fermented soybean, Jeju abalone with watermelon. Everything, from the word "Ato" (gift) to the interiors, is crafted by Korean makers.

jean-georges-new-york-ny.text: Since 1997, Jean-Georges Vongerichten's flagship overlooking Columbus Circle has served the lighter, brighter French cooking that made his name — stocks and cream traded for herbal vinaigrettes and vegetable-forward plates with Asian accents. Two Michelin stars and a longtime four-star New York Times rating attest to its staying power. Signatures endure: egg toast with caviar, foie gras with sour-cherry granola, and tuna ribbons that have been on the menu for more than two decades, capped by his famous molten chocolate cake.

masa-new-york-ny.text: Masayoshi Takayama's Masa is New York's most expensive restaurant, an austere Columbus Circle sanctuary built around a $260,000 slab of hinoki cypress and fish flown in daily from Japan. First in the U.S. to hold three Michelin stars for sushi — a title it kept fifteen years before moving to two in 2025 — it remains a singular omakase of foie gras nigiri, Masa toro crowned with osetra caviar, and otherworldly abalone. Seatings run from $750 to a $1,200 seasonal omakase; there is no menu, only Masa.

chef-s-table-at-brooklyn-fare-new-york-n.text: Chef's Table at Brooklyn Fare began beside a Brooklyn grocery store and became the first NYC restaurant outside Manhattan to earn three Michelin stars, later moving to a counter in Hell's Kitchen. After founding chef César Ramirez departed in 2023, owner Moe Issa reopened it under co-executive chefs Max Natmessnig and Marco Prins, and Michelin re-awarded two stars. The format holds: an intimate counter and a seafood-forward, seasonal tasting menu served to just a handful of guests.

gabriel-kreuther-new-york-ny.text: Across from Bryant Park in Midtown, Gabriel Kreuther brings the Alsatian-born chef's homeland to a polished two-star dining room marked by his signature stork motif. Kreuther's cooking is rooted in classic French technique with an Alsatian heart — a warm kugelhopf with chive fromage blanc, a smoked-sturgeon-and-sauerkraut tart, and foie gras in myriad guises, seared with quince and chestnut or tucked beside squab. An old-school cheese trolley and a deep list of Alsatian wines complete the ritual.

saison-san-francisco-ca.text: At Saison, in San Francisco's SoMa, seasonal California ingredients meet smoke and flame across an open wood-fire kitchen. Executive chef Richard Lee builds intimate, live-fire tasting menus, roughly $328 to $500-plus, around vegetables, seafood and meats kissed by the hearth, served to a small room with a six-seat bar and a private kitchen table for those who want to sit closest to the fire. It is an elemental, ingredient-driven expression of Northern California.

blue-hill-at-stone-barns-tarrytown-ny.text: On a working farm in the Hudson Valley, Dan Barber's Blue Hill at Stone Barns turns agriculture into dinner — a two-star, Green-Star kitchen whose sprawling multi-course menu changes daily, even table to table, by whatever the fields and greenhouses offer that morning. Barber has gone so far as to breed vegetables to order, like his heatless Habanada pepper. Less a meal than an edible snapshot of the surrounding farm, it is among the most influential farm-to-table restaurants in America.

the-inn-at-little-washington-washington-.text: Patrick O'Connell opened The Inn at Little Washington in a Virginia crossroads in 1978, determined to bring world-class dining to the American countryside — teaching himself from Julia Child and making pilgrimages to France's great restaurants for a benchmark. Decades on, it is among the most celebrated country inns in the world, serving a regional American cuisine built on local farms and the Inn's own garden. Its menus range from enduring classics — herb-crusted Elysian Fields lamb carpaccio with Caesar-salad ice cream — to butter-poached Maine lobster and a fully vegetarian tasting.
